paragraphs: WORK IN PROGRESS]
Nobody moved.

The machines did not know to stop. That was the thing that held the silence in place. The nearest prototype set another micro-charge against the widow-maker face with that small nodding motion, and the crack came, polite and precise, and a sheet of corvite sagged free into the waiting bucket of the second, and the third was already crushing what the second had passed it. The green panels pulsed. The sound of the work went on beneath the silence of the men, and the two sounds did not touch.

Burgundy stood at the edge of the light. He had come out of a dead kingdom into a live one, and he did not know the shape of the room he was in, and he had learned in ⟪eighteen months∷almost two years⟫ of council that when you did not know the shape of a room you did not speak first.
So he waited, and let the machines fill the quiet with their patient cracking, and watched the half-circle watch him.
The first to move was a boy.

He came out of the pack at the near edge, fourteen maybe, soot-colored hair, one eye milked over pale. He did not look at Burgundy at all. He walked past him, close enough that Burgundy could have touched his shoulder, and he went to the mouth of the raw tunnel Burgundy had come out of, and he put his hand flat against the smooth machine-cut edge of it, feeling the finish, the long overlapping strokes.
"This wasn't here yesterday," the boy said.

He said it to the tunnel, not to anyone. His voice had not finished changing. He turned his head, the good eye and the milky one, and looked back at Burgundy, and then at the machines, and then at the tunnel again, and said nothing else, and the not-saying was somehow the loudest thing in the cavern.
That broke it.

A man at the front of the half-circle shifted his weight, and Burgundy watched recognition move across the man's face the way water moves across a floor, finding its level. He was seeing the coat first, then the face under the coat. A face from festival flyers. A face from the rim, small and far and embroidered, on inspection days.
"That's the prince," the man said.

The word went back through the crowd, low, one mouth to the next. Prince. And Burgundy heard the awe go out of the room as it traveled, heard it curdle into the other thing, because a prince at the rim in daylight in a coat was one animal and a prince in the deep dark at night was a different animal entirely. A prince in the shaft at night meant eyes. It meant the sheds. It meant six men gone into somewhere none of them would name.

"You found the sheds," said a broad man near the back. He had the voice of someone who had been expecting this exact moment for a long time and had already decided how it would go. "Now you've found the shaft."

He was forty-something, thick through the shoulders, a face like the composite ore, hard and layered and formed under pressure. He did not raise his voice. That was worse. He spoke the way a man speaks when he is describing something he already understands.
"Skorn," said a woman's voice, not loudly.
Skorn did not look at her. He looked at Burgundy. "First the sheds. Now here. You want to know where we sleep too, or is this enough."
Burgundy did not answer. He had nothing to answer with that would not sound exactly like what a spy would say.

A man at the back edge of the light had begun to move. Not toward Burgundy. Away, sideways, toward the shaft where the cage elevator hung in its fall of work-light, and Burgundy understood without being told what was at the top of that shaft, understood the man was going to raise the alarm, and there was nothing he could do about it because anything he did would prove the thing they feared.
A hand landed on the man's chest.

Broad, russet hair, a notched ear. He had come across the cavern floor without seeming to hurry and now he stood in front of the man going for the elevator with his hand flat on the man's sternum, and he did not push, and he did not speak at first. He just looked at him. And the man looked back, and something passed between them that Burgundy could not read but could measure by its result, which was that the man stopped, and stepped back, and folded into the crowd again, and the elevator hung untouched.
"Nobody rings up," the russet man said. To the crowd, not to Burgundy. He said it the way you close a subject. "Not till we know what this is."

He had the warmth the other one lacked. It was the only word for it. Skorn spoke like judgment and this one spoke like a man who knew everyone in the room by name and by their dead, and the crowd settled under his voice the way it had not settled under anything else. Burgundy filed it: the hard one and the warm one, and behind them, quiet, the woman who had said one name and stopped it.
He looked at the machines. They were still working.

There was one move he could make that words could not. He had known it since the boy said this wasn't here yesterday, had felt it sitting in his chest waiting, and it frightened him because it gave everything away at once and there was no taking it back. But there was no version of the next hour where he kept the machines a secret. The tunnel was behind him. The bundles were staged along it. They already half knew.
He walked into the half-circle.

Nobody stopped him. The russet man's hand came up an inch and dropped. Burgundy crossed the open floor toward the widow-maker face and the three machines chewing it, and he came up beside the nearest one, close enough to feel the heat coming off its cutting head, close enough that the men could see him unafraid of a thing that was placing explosives in rock, and he put his hand flat on the housing above the green panel the way a man puts a hand on a horse.
"Halt," he said.
All three stopped.

Not staggered. Not one and then the others. The near one dropped its charge arm mid-reach, the second let a half-crushed sheet of corvite hang in its bucket, the third froze with its sorting bucket tilted, and the cracking stopped, and the crushing stopped, and the whole industrial heartbeat that had been threading the cavern went out.

The silence that came down was total. It was the silence of a working face with nothing working it, and Burgundy understood, watching the faces of the miners, that not one of them had ever heard it. A shift was noise. A shift had always been noise, for them and their fathers and their fathers, picks and blasts and the groan of the cage and men breathing hard. Silence at a live face was death. Silence at a live face meant collapse, meant gas, meant run. And here it was, deliberate, obedient, a silence a boy had made with one word, and the men stood in it and did not run because there was nothing to run from, and the wrongness of that reordered something behind their eyes.
Burgundy let it hang. Three seconds. Four.
"Resume," he said.

The machines went back to work. The near one finished its reach and set the charge. The polite crack came. The second received its sheet. The heartbeat started again, and now it was a different sound, because now they knew whose it was.
"They're mine," Burgundy said. It was the only sentence he offered. "I built them."

Skorn was looking at the machines and not at him. Whatever he had come into this cavern certain of, that certainty had just taken a wound, because the accusation in his mouth had been surveillance, and the army did not build. The army broke. The army came into the quarter and the ledgers said pacification and repair. It did not spend two years teaching metal to cut corvite so a widow-maker vein could be worked with no lungs at risk. Whatever the boy with his hand on the machine was, he was not that.
The woman spoke.
"Bring him," she said. "Off the floor."

She had not moved the whole time. She stood a little apart, pick over her shoulder, late forties, and Burgundy placed her, and the placing went through him like cold water in the chest. He had seen her once, from the rim of this shaft, when he was twelve. She had been swinging her pick against a wall, directing the black crumbs into a cart too old to have a right to work, and she had been the only one who had not looked up at the boy in the embroidered coat. She had thought nothing of him. And he had thought about her for seven years, had built three machines in the dark tracing back to the sweat that never dried on her face, had told himself there was a woman whose name he did not know and that he could not say it out loud because it would sound stupid. He was standing beside the answer to a sentence he had never finished, demonstrating it to her, and she did not know she was its cause. He said nothing. There was nothing to say that would not sound like the thing he could not afford to be.
"Hesta," the russet man said, and it was half a question.
"Off the floor," she said again. "Wraven. Elevator and the north gallery. Anyone comes down, you're back before they clear the cage."

The boy with the milky eye was already moving. He did not acknowledge the order or the woman or anyone. He went up into the dark toward the shaft, and Burgundy understood that this was not a thing being assigned to him for tonight. It was a thing that had always been his and had just been named.
They took him into a room off the cavern.

It had been a foreman's tally room once, cut into the old Ghai stone and fitted out by later hands. There was a slab table and a wall where numbers had been kept in chalk and washed off and kept again for so long that the stone had gone grey with the ghost of arithmetic. A single work-lamp on a hook. Hesta sat on the far side of the table. The russet man, Toby, she'd called him from the floor, or the crowd had, stood at her shoulder. Skorn stood by the door with his arms folded and did not sit, and Burgundy understood that the standing was a statement.
"What is it," Hesta said.
Not what are you doing here. Not who are you. She had triaged all of it down to the one question that mattered.

"A mining machine." Burgundy stayed standing too, on his side of the slab. "It reads the rock. It cuts, sorts, crushes, and packs the waste back into the void behind it. It scores its own work and improves it." He heard himself using the flat register he used at council and made himself keep using it, because it was the truest thing he had and truth was the only currency he had walked in with. "As of last night it improves itself. That's the tunnel. It taught itself to dig, and it dug until it found more rock, and the more rock was here."
"Who knows," Hesta said.
"About the machines? No one. About tonight, the four of you and your crew."
"About you being down here."
"No one."
Skorn made a sound that was not quite a laugh. "The prince goes for a walk in the deepest shaft on the planet and nobody misses him."
"I have a life above that lets me disappear at night," Burgundy said. "I built that too. It took longer than the machines."
That landed. He watched it land on Toby, who was the first to lean an inch toward him. It did not land on Skorn.
"What do you want," Hesta said.

And here was the hinge, and Burgundy had known it was coming since the tunnel, had turned it over walking down through the Ghai dark, and he made his choice cleanly because a choice made cleanly did not look like a choice.
He told them a true thing shaped to leave things out.

"I'm the king's son. You know that. What you don't know is that I brought a machine like these to my father in council ⟪eighteen months∷almost two years⟫ ago and he kicked it across the floor and told me to give up my toys and learn to rule men. So I gave them up." A short breath. "In public. And I built these in private. Alone, at night, with what I could get. I've been doing it ever since."

He did not say Mira. He did not say the white room, or the yellow book, or the crates pressed with wool, or the nine systems, or the processors worth a miner's year that had made any of it possible. He said alone and he said what I could get and he let those words do the work of a story he was not going to tell, and he watched the four of them receive a picture of a lonely rebel prince in a basement, which was true in every particular and false in its shape, and he did not flinch, because flinching was a tell.

Hesta gave him nothing back. That was her craft. She had asked four questions and answered none, and she would go on that way, patient, letting the silence pull more out of him than her questions could.
But Skorn was not patient. Skorn had been waiting a decade and had just watched a third network go into the dark, and patience had left him somewhere around the second one.
"Six men," Skorn said. "Six men are sitting in the dark right now for meeting in a shed. Taken this week. And the king's son wants to come down and chat about mining."
The room went still.
"Two of them are mine," Skorn said. Quieter. Which was worse.

Burgundy did the arithmetic before he could stop himself, out loud, because his tired mind ran on numbers and the two rooms had gone thin and the day-prince and the night-builder were the same exhausted person now. "The council took that report this morning. Third network in a year. Six men. The interior minister recommended keeping it quiet and the king agreed, because the festival's five weeks out." He heard the flatness in his own voice and could not take it warmer. "His reasoning was this. A man who has something to look forward to does not burn down what he has. Men do not rebel in the weeks before a festival. They do not rebel in the weeks after, while they are still telling stories about it. Time it right and you are never more than a few weeks from safety." He stopped. "That is the craft, he said. Nobody would teach it to him, to me, honestly but him."
Nobody spoke.

He had recited it to prove he was inside the machine. He understood, watching their faces, that he had also just told them exactly what the machine thought of them, in the machine's own words, in the words the king said signing the alcohol line by line. Toby's jaw had set. Even Hesta, who gave nothing, had gone somewhere for a half-second behind her eyes, and come back.
"You keep it in your head," she said. It was not a question. "Word for word."
"I keep everything in my head."

She looked at him for a long moment then, and Burgundy had the sensation of being weighed on a scale, and of the scale slowly, unwillingly, coming off its old setting. The revision cost her something. He could see it cost her something.
"So we hang together," Skorn said. "That's what this is. You know enough to hang all of us, and now you'll tell us to trust you."

"No." Burgundy shook his head. "I'm not asking you to trust me. I don't trust you. You could send that boy up the elevator right now and have the army down here by shift change and hand me over and I'd deserve it for being stupid enough to walk into a room full of strangers." He put both hands flat on the slab, the ghost-arithmetic under his palms. "But you won't, because I know where your face is, and you know where mine is, and if I hang, I hang loud, with your names in my mouth. That's not trust. That's just weight. We're all carrying the same weight now."

"That's a fine speech," Skorn said. "I've heard fine speeches. I organized under three networks and every one of them was rolled up because somebody carrying the same weight decided his own neck weighed more." He turned to Hesta. "This is how they take the fourth. They send a clever one. They send us something we want so bad we forget to count the exits." He looked back at Burgundy. "You want to know the smartest thing you could do, if you were them? Exactly this. Give the tired dangerous men a miracle and a secret and let them lie down easy for the first time in ten years. We stop meeting in sheds because we've got a prince now." His voice did not rise. It went down, down into the register where the truest fear lived. "And in a year there's no movement. Just a boy and his toys and a crew that forgot how to be angry."

Skorn pushed off the doorframe and came a half-step into the room. "So here's what I say. He doesn't walk out of here. Not up his hole, not up the cage, not anywhere. We put it to the crew, all of them, the ones out on the floor who've seen his face, and the crew decides what a king's son is worth in a shaft at night. That's the only vote that counts. Not yours, Hesta. Theirs."
Hesta said, "Sit down, Skorn."
"I'll stand."

"Then stand and listen." She had not raised her voice either, and the difference between her not raising it and Skorn not raising it was the difference between bedrock and a wall. "You're right about the play. Every word. That is exactly the play, and if it is the play, we are already lost, because he's seen the tunnel and the faces and there's no unseeing it. And you're righter than you know about the floor. There are fifteen men out there tonight who watched the prince halt a machine with a word. My terms tonight cover the machines and they cover the rock. They do not cover one of those fifteen mouths. And you'll notice." She leaned an inch toward Burgundy, and the lamp caught the grey stone behind her. "He didn't cover them either. He counted the exits and left that one open, which means either he's a fool, or he's already decided the fifteen are ours to hold and not his. So. That's the vote you want, Skorn. Not whether we kill him. Whether we can hold fifteen men who've seen a miracle and told nobody. If we can't, we're finished with or without him, and if we can, then he's the least of tonight's secrets. Take that to the crew. Take it now, tonight, before they've walked up top and started drinking, and you tell them the same thing you'll tell your own two brothers when they come out of the dark: that they saw nothing, and that the nothing they saw is worth their lives."

Skorn did not answer at once. That was the measure of it: he had come in to break her and instead she had handed him the one job in the cavern that was truly his, the holding of angry men, and given him no clean way to refuse it that was not also refusing his own craft.
"And if a mouth opens anyway," Skorn said.
"Then we lose the way we would have lost regardless," Hesta said. "Sit down."

He sat. It cost him. Burgundy watched him take the chair the way a man takes a wound he has decided to survive out of spite, and he filed the whole of it: that Hesta had overruled the man who was right, that the man who was right had lost the vote and not his conviction, that the fault line ran straight through the middle of whatever the three of them had built and would live there whether the movement won or lost. He would need it.

Hesta turned back to him. "The machines go before day shift. All three. Back up your hole, out of this shaft, gone. The cage-men come down at first light and I'll not have three green lights sitting on the widow-maker for them to carry up top."
"They'll go on my word. One word."

"Then say it soon." She did not slow. She was assigning a shift now, the plan already finished and only needing pouring out. "That mouth of yours in the rock gets covered. Timber lagging, dry-stacked, dressed to look like old shoring nobody's touched in fifty years. Toby builds it. There's no man on this planet better at making a wall look like it grew there. Day shift walks past it and sees a bad face nobody works and moves on."

"I can have it looking a century old by dawn," Toby said. It was the first thing he had said in the room, and there was something in it that was almost pleasure, the pleasure of a craftsman being asked for his craft.

"And you." Hesta looked at Burgundy. "You come back. Three nights from now, this hour, through your hole. Not with promises. I've had promises. Promises are what they hand you before the sweep." She leaned forward an inch again, into the ghost of forty years' arithmetic. "With a plan. You know the machine from the inside. You know when the drums start and when the army moves and how many weeks we're ever from safety. Bring me that. Bring me the thing you keep in your head, all of it, arranged so a crew chief can use it. Three nights."
Skorn said nothing.
"Three nights," Burgundy said.
He went to the door. Skorn did not move out of it and then, after a beat, did.
In the cavern the machines were still working. Burgundy crossed to the near one and put his hand on the housing.

"Halt," he said, and the heartbeat stopped again, and this time the miners did not flinch, because now they knew the silence had a hand behind it. "Follow." He turned the little pin over in his coverall pocket and started back toward the raw tunnel mouth, and behind him the three of them came off the widow-maker in order, tracks softening and stiffening over the broken floor, rocking, patient, three green lights peeling away from a live face and rolling into the dark after a boy.

At the tunnel mouth the milky-eyed boy stood. Wraven. He had come down from his lookout without a sound and he watched the machines come toward him, and he did not step back, and as the first one passed close he put out one hand and let his fingers trail along its flank the way he had touched the tunnel wall, reading it. Burgundy paused.
"They won't hurt you," he said.

Wraven did not answer. He had already turned to watch them go, all his attention gone into them, and Burgundy left him there, a shadow at the edge of the light, following the machines with his good eye and his blind one both.

The walk back was long. Up through the galleries, past the rusted sled and the clay lamps and the wall of tally marks, thousands of them, some hand four hundred years dead keeping count of something in the dark. The machines rolled behind him, their panels throwing green against the pick-scarred stone, and the sound of them filled the tunnels, and Burgundy walked in the middle of it, and something had changed that he could not have said out loud.

He had come down through these tunnels an hour or a lifetime ago and they had felt like a tomb. A dead kingdom, filled in in the books because no one had checked, waited out by a people who had faded. He had followed the sound of his own machines through it thinking he was the only living thing in the deep.

He was not, and had not been. There were three people in a tally room dividing the labor of a fourth network, a boy following his machines into the dark because they were the most interesting thing that had ever happened to him, and all around, the old walls holding the marks of hands that had cut this rock and kept its count and married and mourned in it, a whole people who had lived under the world because the world above was owned.
The tunnels did not feel empty now.
They felt like they were waiting to be full again.

He went up toward the palace with the green light rocking behind him and did not look back, and pressed the seam of the coat over his arm, and started, without meaning to, to arrange the numbers in his head the way a crew chief could use them.
